title: I Found My CEO Asleep on My Couch After Halloween… Wearing My Hoodie and Hugging a Teddy Bear.

blocks.text: “You slept with the CEO, so your career is over,” Victor Hensley said, shoving a photograph across the conference table. My boss was in it, leaving my apartment in my hoodie. He figured that picture would destroy both of us. He hadn’t counted on a pink confession card, a teddy bear wearing a construction helmet, or the county deed buried beneath a fake sale agreement. By Friday, a children’s center was facing demolition, a woman had supposedly signed legal documents while under anesthesia, and I had a job offer in Chicago that could get me out of the mess completely. All I had to do was walk away. I didn’t.
At Sunday morning, I found my CEO asleep on my couch, wearing my favorite navy hoodie and hugging a teddy bear with a plastic construction helmet.
Then a folded pink card slipped out of her pocket.
“Please tell me that’s not my termination notice,” I muttered.
She saw the card in my hand, sat straight up, and whispered, “Oh, crap.”
Not exactly the reaction you want from a woman you’ve secretly loved for eleven months.
My name is Nolan Avery. I’m thirty-one, single, and until that morning, the most embarrassing thing in my life was accidentally calling a city inspector “Dad” during a zoning meeting.
I’m a senior architectural designer at Hearthline Architecture in Portland, Oregon.
Margot founded the company four years earlier.
She’s twenty-nine, brilliant, terrifying during budget meetings, and capable of making a room full of wealthy developers shut up by setting down her coffee.
She’s also the woman who once drove forty minutes through freezing rain to deliver groceries to our receptionist after her husband was hospitalized.
My hoodie swallowed her hands. Her dark hair stuck out in three different directions.
I’d seen this woman negotiate contracts worth millions without blinking.
Apparently, a four-dollar greeting card could take her down.
“Sure. Maybe start with why you’re sleeping with Inspector Buttons.”
“He’s a respected structural consultant.”
The bear had come from Saturday night’s Halloween fundraiser for Maple Street House, a community center in North Portland.
A little boy had decorated him with a construction helmet and announced that architects needed hugs because their buildings kept falling down.
I’d paid eighty dollars at the charity auction for him.
Margot hadn’t known I was the winning bidder.
She’d been busy arguing with our chief financial officer, Victor Hensley.
Victor was fifty-three, wore suits that cost more than my monthly rent, and treated every nonprofit project like a contagious disease.
Maple Street House was his latest obsession.
“Old buildings don’t need saving,” he’d announced at the party. “They need someone smart enough to sell the land.”
Margot had told him the building wasn’t for sale.
Unfortunately, Saturday night had seemed perfectly harmless.
I wore a cardboard lighthouse costume. Margot wore black cat ears and a little gold bell around her neck.
At midnight, she found my car keys underneath an auction table.
When she showed up at my apartment, the rain was coming down hard enough to turn my driveway into a creek.
We drank chamomile tea. I gave her my hoodie because she was freezing.
She’d apparently moved to the couch, picked up the bear, and stayed.
Now she held out her hand toward the card.
Instead of taking it, she said, “I actually came here for two reasons.”
“I wrote that card two weeks ago. I’ve carried it around like an idiot ever since.”
“Please read it before I lose my nerve.”
Two sentences. Blue ink. Her careful handwriting.
I’ve had feelings for you for a long time.
My brain temporarily stopped functioning.
Margot watched me like she was waiting for a judge to announce a sentence.
“I’ve wanted to ask you out since last Thanksgiving.”
“Remember when I asked whether you knew where the office stapler was?”
“It was supposed to be coffee. The stapler came out instead.”
She laughed so hard she nearly dropped the bear.
“I don’t want anyone thinking you felt pressured.”
“And I don’t want you accused of promoting me because you like how I look in a lighthouse costume.”
“That costume was objectively terrible.”
She smiled again, but we both understood the problem.
Margot approved company budgets. She influenced staffing. She could make decisions affecting my career.
I wasn’t going to pretend that didn’t matter just because I wanted to kiss her.
So I sat beside her and told her the truth.
“I want to say yes. More than you know. But we need to handle the work situation first.”
“I already read our conflict-of-interest policy.”
“That might be the most romantic thing anybody’s ever said to me.”
When I asked whether I could kiss her forehead, she nodded.
But afterward, neither of us moved for several seconds.
I informed her that being a CEO didn’t qualify her to operate kitchen appliances.
She stole another piece of toast and called me insubordinate.
For one ordinary Sunday morning, everything felt ridiculously good.
